Division III

Border Law, Citizenship and Mobility

Section 142.9

The Jay Treaty and Indigenous Border-Crossing Rights

The Jay Treaty was signed in London on November 19, 1794, by representatives of Great Britain and the United States. It addressed unresolved issues arising from American independence, including British military posts, commerce and other disputes between the two countries. In the Great Lakes and northeastern regions, trade and movement across the boundary were particularly important. Neither country could simply treat that boundary as an absolute barrier without disrupting existing commercial and social relationships. Article III of the treaty expressly addressed people described in the treaty as Indians living on either side of the line, as well as British subjects and United States citizens. Its importance for Indigenous history is that it recognized movement across a line that had been negotiated without Indigenous peoples as parties. [2][3]

Article III provided for passage and inland navigation between the territories of the contracting parties, subject to the article's qualifications, and for certain forms of commerce. It also contained specific provisions concerning customs and Indigenous goods. The 1796 explanatory article responded to concerns that trade-licensing provisions of the Treaty of Greenville might interfere with the earlier arrangements. These documents reveal a diplomatic relationship in which the United States and Britain sought to reconcile territorial claims with commerce across a boundary that intersected established Indigenous relationships. They should not be read as a modern immigration statute. Their language, territorial exceptions and provisions concerning trade belong to the circumstances of the late eighteenth century. [3][32]

For many Indigenous nations, the historical importance of the treaty differs from the significance assigned to it by the two contracting states. Indigenous political claims often begin with the premise that the border did not create the right to maintain relationships across a homeland. From this perspective, an interstate treaty acknowledging free passage recognized an existing relationship rather than creating Indigenous nationhood or mobility. State courts, however, ask different questions when determining whether a historical treaty is enforceable within a particular domestic legal system. They may consider later statutes, the constitutional treatment of treaties, the effects of intervening conflicts, and rules governing judicial remedies. The Indigenous understanding of the origin of a right and a judicial determination of its present enforceability are therefore distinct historical subjects.

In the United States, twentieth-century immigration restrictions generated important legal disputes. In McCandless v. United States ex rel. Diabo, decided by a federal appellate court in 1928, Paul Diabo, a Mohawk ironworker from Canada, challenged the application of immigration restrictions to him. The court upheld the lower court's decision in his favor. Congress also enacted legislation on April 2, 1928 (45 Stat. 401), protecting passage for American Indians born in Canada while excluding those whose membership in Indigenous tribes or families arose through adoption. The explicit fifty-percent ancestry threshold belongs to the 1952 statute, not the original 1928 wording. The historical context was the development of national immigration law, including the restrictive Immigration Act of 1924. The case and legislation illustrate the way in which an older history of mobility acquired a new legal expression as states attempted to regulate entry more comprehensively. [33][34][58][55]

The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 carried this statutory protection forward in Section 289, now codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1359. The provision protects passage across the borders of the United States for American Indians born in Canada who meet the statutory minimum of fifty percent American Indian ancestry, expressed in the law in the historical language of blood. The requirement is a federal immigration classification. It is not a definition of Indigenous nationhood and does not determine membership under a nation's own laws. Birth in Canada and the statutory ancestry qualification are distinct from Canadian citizenship or registration under Canada's Indian Act. Federal regulations, including 8 C.F.R. Part 289, address the implementation of the provision and lawful admission for permanent residence. [60] The legal discussion here is historical and institutional, not instructions for individual travel. [35]

The distinction became important in cases involving employment and residence. A federal district court in Akins v. Saxbe (1974), examining the legislative history of Section 289, recognized the rights of qualifying persons to enter and remain in the United States and engage in employment. The case shows why the significance of admission is wider than the act of crossing a line: meaningful mobility can involve living, working and maintaining relationships on either side. Nevertheless, one judicial decision about the operation of a particular statute is not a general declaration that every Indigenous person has an unconditional right to enter the United States. The scope of the law must be understood in relation to the statutory criteria and later legal developments. [34]

Canada developed a different approach. The Supreme Court of Canada in Francis v. The Queen (1956) addressed the enforceability of Jay Treaty customs provisions in Canadian domestic law. It did not recognize the treaty as automatically creating an enforceable customs exemption. Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, enacted in 2001, provides in Section 19(1) for entry and continued presence in Canada for Canadian citizens and persons registered under the Indian Act, in accordance with the Act. It does not reproduce the United States' fifty-percent ancestry test. The absence of identical statutory protection for all related communities has been an important subject of Indigenous advocacy. [36][37][38]

Thus the phrase Jay Treaty rights can refer to several different things: an eighteenth-century diplomatic document, an Indigenous political interpretation, a United States immigration statute, a claim about trade, or a broader demand for reciprocal recognition. A responsible historical analysis identifies which meaning is being used. It also asks who may establish eligibility, what kind of evidence a government recognizes, and whether the claim concerns personal admission, employment, residence, property or another subject. As the following sections demonstrate, crossing rights cannot be understood without these distinctions.

The legal contrast between the two countries also explains why a historical right may acquire an administrative burden. A state agency applying a statutory eligibility criterion requires evidence that the criterion is satisfied. The kind of evidence it accepts may differ from evidence that an Indigenous government uses to establish citizenship. Historical birth records and ancestry records can be incomplete, especially where administrative systems changed over time or failed to record Indigenous people consistently. The issue is not simply inconvenience. It is the relationship between the authority to define a legal category and the ability of individuals to establish that they fall within it. Students should not infer from the statutory rule that the government is competent to decide every question of Indigenous identity.

Legal History Study — Treaty, legislation, judgment and administration

The same phrase, Jay Treaty rights, can identify an Indigenous interpretation, a treaty provision or a modern statutory claim. Compare the 1794 treaty, the 1796 explanatory article, Diabo’s litigation and the 1952 statute. The question of whether a person is entitled to enter a country differs from whether goods are exempt from duties. [3][32][33][35]

  1. Distinguish the date and authority of the treaty from the 1952 statute.
  2. What is the statutory classification under Section 289, and why is it not a definition of Indigenous citizenship?
  3. Why does recognition of passage not necessarily establish an exemption for goods?
Primary Source Window — Article III of the Jay Treaty

Context and source type: Anglo-American Treaty of Amity, Commerce and Navigation signed on 19 November 1794; explanatory article agreed in 1796.

Documentary paraphrase: Article III addresses movement by land or inland waters for specified groups, including Indigenous people living on both sides of the boundary, and contains trade provisions and qualifications.

Analysis: The diplomatic recognition of movement across the line is historically significant; later domestic statutes and judicial decisions must be studied independently.

Perspective and limitations: The signatories were Britain and the United States. The original text does not describe every modern legal entitlement, and it is not an agreement signed by Indigenous nations.

Section 142.10

Indigenous Citizenship and State Citizenship

Indigenous citizenship concerns the political relationship between a person and an Indigenous nation or community. State citizenship concerns a legal relationship between a person and a modern state. Although the two relationships often coexist, neither is simply a synonym for the other. The historical development of the international boundary made the distinction particularly consequential because state governments increasingly required individuals to demonstrate a recognized status before entering, residing or working in their territories. An Indigenous community whose membership extends across the boundary may consequently encounter several different governmental definitions of who its members are.

In the United States, the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 extended United States citizenship to Native people born within the territorial limits of the country who were not already citizens, without extinguishing tribal property rights. Many Indigenous individuals had acquired United States citizenship through earlier processes. The law did not make tribal political membership unnecessary, nor did it erase the distinctions among Indigenous governments. The historical issue was not simply admission into the American political community but the relationship between that admission and continuing tribal nationhood. For a person born outside the United States, Indigenous citizenship alone does not establish citizenship under the laws of the United States.[56]

In Canada, registration under the Indian Act is a legal classification administered through federal law. It must be distinguished from membership or citizenship determined by First Nations themselves. Not every Indigenous person in Canada is registered under the Act: Inuit and Métis have distinct legal and political histories, and even among First Nations people registration and community membership need not coincide. The historical consequences of discriminatory registration rules, including rules affecting women and their descendants, illustrate the importance of distinguishing a government's administrative categories from Indigenous self-determination. Chapter 144 will examine these controversies more fully. The specific importance here is that registration is one of the statuses recognized for entry under Section 19 of Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. [37]

Mexico's constitutional framework recognizes Indigenous peoples and communities and provides for autonomy under the constitutional order. As Chapter 141 explained, the 2024 constitutional reform substantially developed legal recognition of Indigenous peoples and communities. Such recognition differs from United States federal recognition of tribal governments. It is not a separate Mexican immigration nationality. In Greenland, Indigenous identity and political participation operate within a self-government framework in the Kingdom of Denmark. Neither Kalaallit identity nor participation in Greenlandic institutions establishes an automatic right to enter Canada or the United States. These comparisons illustrate the danger of applying one country's categories to the peoples of another.

The statutory ancestry requirement in United States immigration law provides a particularly revealing example. A Canadian-born person may be a citizen of an Indigenous nation yet not meet the ancestry requirement of Section 289. Conversely, meeting the statutory ancestry criterion does not automatically establish citizenship in a particular Indigenous government. An external government may seek evidence of ancestry or birth, while an Indigenous nation's membership rules may emphasize different criteria. This mismatch is historically important because it transfers a question of admission to a state-defined system that does not necessarily reflect the political understandings of the community concerned. The chapter uses the statutory terminology only where necessary to describe the law, not as a scientific classification of Indigenous identity. [35]

Identification documents are another point at which these systems interact. A document issued by an Indigenous government may provide evidence of membership, identity or eligibility for a specific program, while a national passport normally serves a different function. State agencies determine which documents they accept for particular administrative purposes. Some governments have negotiated arrangements concerning Indigenous-issued credentials, but acceptance of one document in one context does not guarantee acceptance of all similar documents elsewhere. The Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative, implemented in stages during the 2000s, exemplifies the increasing emphasis on specified identity and citizenship documents at United States borders. These administrative developments help explain why the relationship between political belonging and physical movement became more consequential. [54][54]

For historians, the relevant question is not which form of citizenship is more authentic. It is how different forms of political membership developed, what rights and obligations they carry, and what happens when their categories conflict. A person can possess several meaningful political relationships while being subject to different territorial regimes. An Indigenous government can maintain a citizenship system that includes people living outside its recognized territory. Understanding these distinctions enables students to interpret border law without adopting external administrative definitions as the measure of Indigenous nationhood.

The consequences of citizenship should also be separated by subject. Political membership can establish a relationship to an Indigenous government's institutions; state citizenship ordinarily establishes a national political status; residence may determine access to a service; and a particular immigration provision may affect permission to remain or work. Even within one country, different agencies may administer these matters under different laws. A person who is recognized for one purpose need not be recognized in the same way for another. This is why the chapter's comparison of documents and citizenship is institutional rather than a comparison of competing identities.

Institutional Study — Political membership and legal status

Indigenous citizenship, state citizenship, Indian Act registration and immigration eligibility serve different institutional purposes. A person can be recognized under several categories, or recognized by an Indigenous government without fitting a state-defined immigration classification. Figure 9 represents two political relationships, not an automatic equivalence between them.

  1. Which government defines each category?
  2. Explain why a national passport and a community membership document serve different purposes.
  3. Why would a historical analysis of mobility be misleading if it used the categories interchangeably?
Historical Vocabulary — Indigenous citizenship

Definition: Political membership in an Indigenous nation or community under its own laws and practices.

Historical context: It exists alongside state citizenship and distinct statutory classifications.

Significance and potential misunderstanding: Indigenous citizenship is not the same as ancestry, national citizenship or federal immigration eligibility.

Section 142.11

Immigration Law and the Right to Cross

Immigration law did not create the movement of people across North America. Migration, trade, seasonal harvesting and family movement long predated modern national admission regimes. As states consolidated their control over territory, however, they increasingly distinguished among citizens, immigrants, temporary visitors, workers and persons excluded from entry. That development changed the practical circumstances of Indigenous communities whose political and cultural relationships extended beyond the territory of a single state. A journey that one generation understood primarily as movement among relatives could become subject to documentation and legal classifications in another generation.

The northern boundary is distinguished by a particular statutory history in the United States. Section 289 of the Immigration and Nationality Act applies to qualifying Canadian-born American Indians. It is not a general provision covering all Indigenous peoples of North America, and its eligibility test must not be confused with a community's own criteria for citizenship. Canada uses a different statutory framework under Section 19 of its Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. These differences can produce asymmetrical outcomes: the legal basis for entering one country may not be available when traveling in the opposite direction. A historical explanation of Indigenous mobility must therefore identify both the destination government and the particular legal relationship of the traveler to that government. [35][37]

The southern border lacks an identical general counterpart to Section 289 for Indigenous people born in Mexico. The Tohono O'odham and Kumeyaay cases demonstrate why this matters. Their historical territories and cultural relationships extend across the boundary, but the national immigration laws governing travel are not determined solely by that historical relationship. Individual circumstances may differ according to citizenship, immigration status and documentation. Negotiated arrangements and particular accommodations must be distinguished from legislation conferring a generally applicable right. The historical contrast with the Canadian-born classification reflects the development of different legal traditions rather than an inherent difference in the legitimacy of Indigenous territorial relationships.

The Texas Band of Kickapoo Act, Public Law 97-429, enacted on January 8, 1983, addressed the situation of the Kickapoo community associated with Texas and Mexico. The statute provided a legal framework for the Band's relationship with the federal government, including enrollment arrangements, services and lands. Its provisions concerning eligibility for United States citizenship and passage across the United States–Mexico boundary addressed a particular transnational history. Section 4(c) of the original Act provided a five-year period after publication of the membership roll notice during which enrolled members could apply for U.S. citizenship; section 4(d) provides for passage across U.S. borders and living and working in the United States for members of the Band. This is not automatic dual citizenship for all people of Kickapoo ancestry. The 2024 compilation of Title 25 omits these special provisions as not of general application; omission from that compilation is not itself a repeal. The original enacted text is the appropriate historical reference. [39][52][53]

The statute should be read against the background of nineteenth-century Kickapoo movement and the establishment of the community at El Nacimiento in Coahuila. As Chapter 141 explained, that community's relationship to Texas resulted from migration, political choices and displacement, rather than simply a line dividing a long-established southwestern homeland. Federal legislation in 1983 responded to an existing history that ordinary categories of national residence and citizenship did not fully accommodate. It was therefore an institutional solution to a specific political problem. The fact that Congress created such an arrangement demonstrates the capacity of law to adapt to Indigenous circumstances, but it does not establish that similar arrangements already exist for every other transboundary community.

Admission, residence, employment and access to services should be treated as separate questions. A legal entitlement to enter a country may have consequences for residence and work under a particular legal framework; in other circumstances the permitted activities of a traveler may be limited. Access to healthcare, education or public benefits may be governed by additional laws and administrative systems. The implications of a right to cross cannot be inferred solely from the wording of an international agreement. They depend on the interaction of statutes, regulations, administrative interpretation and the legal status of the person concerned. Students should also distinguish a legally enforceable right from an accommodation that may depend on the exercise of administrative discretion.

Indigenous advocacy concerning these issues has repeatedly challenged the assumption that transboundary movement is comparable in every respect to ordinary international migration. Canadian government consultations documented in 2024 included distinct engagement with First Nations, Inuit and Métis organizations. These consultations addressed problems of mobility, documentation and the movement of goods, while recognizing that the interests of different Indigenous peoples are not identical. Discussions about legislative and policy reform do not themselves establish new legal rights. Their historical importance is that Indigenous organizations have placed the inadequacy of existing national classifications on the governmental agenda. [38]

The original Kickapoo statute also addressed service delivery, authorizing provision of federal Indian programs and services to the Band and its members in Maverick County without the usual dependence on the existence of a reservation or nearby residence. Section 7(b) called for consultation and cooperation with appropriate Mexican governmental bodies to address the community's distinctive needs. The legislation therefore addressed more than immigration. It recognized that land, mobility and public services were interrelated institutional problems. This feature distinguishes the statute from a narrow exception dealing only with entry at a port of entry. [39]

Comparative Legal Study — Different foundations of border mobility

Compare Section 289 of the U.S. Immigration and Nationality Act, Section 19 of Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, and Section 4 of the Texas Band of Kickapoo Act. The instruments have different criteria and histories. They are not interchangeable travel permissions. [35][37][39]

  2. Why should the historical five-year Kickapoo citizenship application period be distinguished from the separate passage provision?
  3. Identify one question not answered by a provision governing personal admission.

Section 142.12

Customs, Trade and the Movement of Cultural Property

Customs administration developed as governments sought to collect revenue, regulate commercial exchange and protect particular markets. Along North America's international boundaries, these objectives increasingly intersected with Indigenous economic relationships. A bundle of goods moving across a river might represent commercial merchandise to a customs officer, a gift within a kinship network to the person carrying it, or material needed for cultural activity to an Indigenous community. These classifications can have different legal consequences. Understanding a border therefore requires attention to the movement of things as well as the movement of people.

Article III of the Jay Treaty included provisions addressing duties on goods carried by Indigenous people across the boundary. The historical text distinguished Indigenous goods and effects from certain commercial consignments and included qualifications. It must be examined within its eighteenth-century diplomatic and commercial context. A historical provision cannot simply be assumed to establish a modern exemption under every applicable customs law. In Canada, questions about the status of the treaty within domestic law arose in Francis v. The Queen in 1956. In the United States, the statutory protection of personal passage in Section 289 of the Immigration and Nationality Act does not itself create a comprehensive exemption from customs regulation. Personal admission and the treatment of merchandise belong to different administrative and legal systems. In United States v. Garrow (1937), the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals rejected a claim to duty-free entry of baskets from Canada, reasoning that the earlier treaty and statutory exemptions no longer supplied the asserted exemption. That decision illustrates the distinct development of United States customs law, rather than establishing an exceptionless rule about every Indigenous good or treaty. [3][35][36][59]

The Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Mitchell v. M.N.R., 2001 SCC 33, provides a major example. Grand Chief Michael Mitchell of Akwesasne asserted an Aboriginal right to bring goods into Canada from the United States for purposes including trade without paying customs duty. His claim was examined under Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982, rather than being resolved simply by reference to the Jay Treaty. Lower courts had accepted a form of the claim. The Supreme Court ultimately rejected it, finding the historical evidence insufficient to establish the specific asserted practice as an Aboriginal right in the form required by the governing legal test. Some judicial reasoning also addressed the relationship between the claimed right and Canadian sovereignty. The result should not be generalized into a holding that all Indigenous cross-border trade or mobility rights are extinguished. [40]

The case is instructive for historical method as well as law. To identify the historical basis of a claimed right, a court considers evidence concerning practices of the relevant people and their relationship to the claimed activity. Oral history, archaeological evidence and documentary records can all be relevant. A court's evidentiary framework, however, does not exhaust the ways that a community understands its history. The legal outcome of a particular case reflects the issue presented, the evidence admitted and the judicial doctrine applied. It is not an authoritative determination of the totality of a nation's territorial relationships. Historians should distinguish what a judgment establishes in law from the broader historical questions that remain open.

In addition to tariffs and commercial classification, contemporary customs systems interact with agricultural, wildlife and cultural-property regulation. The movement of traditional foods, plant materials, medicines and artistic materials may implicate regulations intended to prevent disease, protect endangered species or control imports. Cultural objects may be subject to other legal requirements. The purpose of a regulation can be legitimate while its application creates substantial difficulties for communities whose obligations cross a border. The historical issue is therefore not whether all regulation should disappear, but how regulatory institutions developed and whether they adequately recognize Indigenous practices and relationships.

Economic exchange also encompasses activities that conventional commercial statistics do not readily capture. Gifts, shared resources and reciprocal obligations may be essential to household and community welfare even when no money changes hands. Conversely, Indigenous-owned businesses may participate in international commerce through the same commercial channels as other enterprises while also supporting distinctive community institutions. A historical analysis must avoid assuming that all Indigenous commerce is either traditional gift exchange or conventional corporate activity. Both forms, and many combinations of them, may exist in the same community. The regulatory treatment of goods can affect these activities differently, making customs a central subject in the history of divided homelands.

The contrast between Francis and Mitchell is historically useful. In the first case, the issue centered on the claimed domestic effect of a treaty provision. In the second, the claim was framed as an Aboriginal right under the Canadian constitutional order. A similar practical concern, the treatment of goods crossing the border, was thus addressed through different legal doctrines in different historical periods. Students should avoid interpreting the second case as merely a repetition of the first. Its constitutional and evidentiary setting was different, and the legal questions examined by the court were correspondingly different.

Multiple Perspectives — Cultural obligations and customs

Community members may understand objects as gifts, teaching materials or elements of ceremonial obligations; customs officials must apply import rules; conservation agencies protect wildlife and agriculture. Indigenous governments may seek arrangements that account for the particular meaning of the objects involved. These are institutional perspectives, not invented testimony from individuals. The Mitchell judgment illustrates a concrete dispute about duties. [40]

Analysis: The decision illustrates the distinction between establishing a particular Aboriginal right in a court and establishing the wider history of Indigenous cross-border relationships.

Division IV

Economic, Social and Administrative Consequences

Section 142.13

Border Administration, Surveillance and Enforcement

The construction of an international boundary involves a sequence of institutional developments. The first may be a diplomatic agreement establishing the line. Surveyors may then identify its location in the landscape. Governments may build facilities for collecting revenue and regulating commerce. As national immigration systems develop, officials acquire responsibilities for determining whether individuals may enter and under what conditions. The physical infrastructure and administrative procedures used to perform these functions change over time. The history of a border is therefore not exhausted by the date on which the treaty establishing it was signed.

In the United States, customs administration dates to the early republic, whereas the federal Border Patrol was established in 1924 as part of a period of increasingly restrictive immigration policy. The twentieth century saw further consolidation of immigration and inspection services. Canada developed its own customs and immigration institutions in relation to Confederation, national economic policy and changing immigration legislation. These developments had different effects along different sections of the border. The Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River were already major commercial corridors, while the southwestern border crossed extensive desert and agricultural regions. Arctic movement involved much different logistical and geopolitical circumstances. Institutional change must therefore be examined in relation to the local geography of each Indigenous community.[57]

After the attacks of September 11, 2001, governments expanded their emphasis on border security, identification and interagency coordination. In the United States, the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection in 2003 reorganized responsibility for border management. During the following years, the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative introduced new documentary requirements for travel to the United States through different modes of transportation. The program and related administrative changes affected many travelers, including Indigenous people. They did not initiate all Indigenous mobility disputes, which long predated 2001, but they altered the institutional context within which those disputes occurred.[54]

Akwesasne demonstrates why administrative changes can have consequences different from those experienced by an ordinary international visitor. Some journeys connecting parts of the community involve travel across international or provincial lines. Residents have therefore had to reconcile community geography with inspection and reporting requirements. The Mohawk Council of Akwesasne has pursued governmental dialogue and legal advocacy concerning these issues. Such negotiations concern not only the convenience of crossing but also the authority of Indigenous governments, the provision of services and the relationship between the community and external agencies. An administrative solution may reduce a particular difficulty while leaving broader questions of Indigenous jurisdiction unresolved. [16][38]

In the southern borderlands, physical infrastructure has become a particularly visible subject of dispute. The Tohono O'odham Nation has distinguished its cooperation with governmental agencies from consent to border-wall construction. Infrastructure can affect access to land, environmental systems and relationships with communities across the boundary. The Nation's public statements emphasize that security decisions concern land over which it has governmental and cultural responsibilities. The historical analysis should take seriously both the state's claimed responsibilities for administering an international boundary and the Indigenous government's responsibilities to its members and territory. Neither objective eliminates the need to examine the jurisdictional relationship between them. [25]

Border enforcement may also produce unequal practical consequences without formally distinguishing among categories of traveler. A documentary requirement that is relatively simple for one person can be difficult for someone whose records are incomplete or whose membership is defined under a different political system. A delay may affect a person traveling for work differently from someone traveling for an urgent family responsibility. Administrative decisions can therefore affect economic and social relationships as well as the formal right to travel. Government consultations concerning Indigenous mobility have identified documentation and inconsistent experiences of administration as continuing issues. Such records provide evidence of institutional problems, not proof that every traveler encounters the same circumstances. [38]

Administrative capacity has a history of its own. The replacement of informal arrangements by standardized procedures can improve consistency in some respects, yet a uniform procedure may fit local circumstances poorly. Indigenous governments whose territories intersect national boundaries may possess knowledge of local conditions that external agencies lack. Consultation and negotiated arrangements can therefore be understood as efforts to adapt a general administrative system to particular political geography. The effectiveness of such efforts must be evaluated in practice rather than inferred from the announcement of a policy or the establishment of a working group.

Cause and Effect — Administrative expansion and mobility

The creation of national boundaries established a territorial framework; customs, immigration, documentary rules and infrastructure gradually transformed movement. Security reforms after 2001 accelerated some administrative changes but did not originate the earlier conflicts over Indigenous mobility. Effects differ according to geography and purpose of travel.

  2. Distinguish a law governing entry from the physical infrastructure used to administer it.
  3. How could Indigenous consultation alter the administration of an existing boundary?
Section 142.14

Families, Kinship and the Everyday Experience of Divided Homelands

International borders reorganize the geography of ordinary responsibilities. Kinship relationships can require travel between households, participation in weddings and funerals, care for elders, support for children and involvement in community events. When relatives live under different national jurisdictions, these responsibilities may require repeated interaction with administrative institutions. The historical significance of mobility therefore cannot be understood exclusively through statistics recording immigration or tourism. Many movements occur because people regard several places as part of their social and political world rather than because they intend to relocate permanently.

Akwesasne provides an especially clear example. Its residents may have relatives, employment or community services in different portions of the territory, and the community's internal geography intersects the international line. The Mohawk Council's description of Akwesasne emphasizes its location in two Canadian provinces and the United States. A person's responsibilities within the community are not necessarily organized according to those administrative divisions. A journey to participate in community life may nevertheless be treated by a state as international travel. The interaction of these two geographies explains why apparently routine border administration can become a substantial part of the everyday historical experience of a divided homeland. [16]

The southern borderlands provide related but distinct examples. Indigenous communities in Sonora, Arizona, Baja California and California have histories of family relationships, movement for work and community participation that developed under changing national arrangements. The Tohono O'odham and Kumeyaay cases should be distinguished from the Kickapoo experience of migration and the creation of new community centers. In each case, however, a person's relationship to an Indigenous community may extend beyond the country in which that person resides. The international boundary can therefore introduce different administrative conditions for maintaining relationships that are understood by community members as part of ordinary social life.

It is important to distinguish several forms of movement. Occasional travel may involve a single event or visit. Seasonal mobility involves recurrent movement tied to employment, harvesting or other recurring activities. Permanent migration involves a change in the principal place of residence. Multilocal residence refers to actually living in more than one location over a period of time; it is not simply a term for having relatives elsewhere. A household may combine these forms of movement. The categories should not be used to impose a uniform interpretation on Indigenous mobility, but they help historians identify which activities were affected by particular changes in law or administration.

The consequences of restrictions may vary according to the resources and circumstances of households. Repeated travel has costs, including transportation, time away from employment and possible administrative expenses. Children and older people may depend on other relatives to travel. People with disabilities or health needs may face additional logistical problems. A family with secure documentation and financial resources may experience a border differently from a family encountering uncertain eligibility or limited transportation. These are analytical considerations rather than claims about every Indigenous household. Historical studies should seek evidence from particular communities and avoid inventing representative personal stories.

Women, elders and young people are also participants in Indigenous political and social life, not merely recipients of border policy. Women may organize cultural programs, advocate for families, operate enterprises and participate in government; elders may serve as knowledge holders and community leaders; young people may develop new ways of maintaining relationships through education and communication. Transboundary programs can help support these responsibilities, but digital communication does not fully substitute for physical presence or access to land. The history of families across borders thus concerns both the practical consequences of regulation and the institutional capacity of communities to sustain relationships across generations.

Family relationships also demonstrate why statistics about international migration cannot capture the entire historical experience of divided communities. Counts of permanent migrants may omit repeated short journeys, unsuccessful efforts to travel, or responsibilities assumed by relatives who live in different places. An ethnographic account or community history can provide evidence of these relationships, but it must not expose private information without permission. A comparative historical study should distinguish publicly documented institutional circumstances from the individual experiences that researchers would need additional ethical evidence to establish.

Everyday Life Study — Family responsibilities across jurisdictions

Use Akwesasne’s publicly documented community geography, rather than an invented biography, to analyze mobility. A journey between parts of a divided community can involve state administration even where the purpose is an ordinary family or community obligation. Consider the cumulative effects of time, cost and documentation. [16]

  1. Compare an occasional visit, seasonal travel and multilocal residence.
  2. How might repeated trips affect household resources differently from a single journey?
  3. What sources could reveal these experiences while protecting private information?
Section 142.15

Borderland Economies, Employment and Indigenous Commerce

The international boundary can function simultaneously as a barrier to economic activity and as a point of connection between markets. Indigenous peoples had developed extensive systems of exchange before modern states, and many subsequently became participants in colonial trade, commercial agriculture, wage employment and other economic institutions. The creation of international boundaries did not eliminate these relationships, but it changed the rules governing access to markets, land, employment and resources. In the Great Lakes, waterways connected commercial centers across the emerging boundary. On the northern Plains, the destruction of the buffalo economy and the expansion of ranching and agriculture profoundly changed the circumstances of Indigenous communities. In the southern borderlands, labor migration and commercial agriculture interacted with the histories of divided and displaced peoples.

Employment illustrates the relationship between legal status and economic opportunity. An individual may belong to a community whose members live on both sides of an international boundary, while the ability to work in either country is governed by particular national legal arrangements. Paul Diabo's case in the 1920s concerned a Mohawk worker from Canada whose circumstances were affected by United States immigration restrictions. Later litigation over the meaning of Section 289 addressed the ability of qualifying Canadian-born Indigenous people to live and work in the United States. The history of Indigenous cross-border labor therefore cannot be explained solely by the economic incentives to seek employment; it also requires analysis of the legal institutions governing movement. [33][34][35]

Migration for agricultural and other work can support households through wages and remittances, but it may also expose workers to insecurity and separate relatives for extended periods. The Kickapoo community's transnational history includes movement between Mexico and the United States. The particular federal arrangements adopted in 1983 are important partly because legal uncertainty can affect the ability of families to sustain economic relationships. These relationships must not be reduced to labor migration alone. The community has its own political, ceremonial and territorial institutions, which shape the purposes and meaning of mobility. Participation in a labor market does not make an Indigenous community simply an immigrant population.

Indigenous-controlled enterprises provide another form of economic agency. A government or community institution may support business development, market cultural products, organize tourism or invest in resource-related enterprises. Such initiatives can strengthen governmental capacity by generating employment, revenue and resources for community programs. At the same time, international regulations and differences in tax, land and business law can affect the feasibility of particular commercial activities. Indigenous businesses must operate within the legal environments relevant to their operations, which may include Indigenous laws as well as state and federal regulations. No single economic model characterizes all transboundary communities.

The treatment of goods discussed in Section 142.12 also affects production and consumption. A restriction on the movement of a material can raise the cost of production for an artist or business; a restriction on harvesting can affect food security and the household economy. Shared ecosystems are particularly important because many Indigenous economic relationships involve renewable resources that move across political jurisdictions. Fishing and wildlife management therefore connect economic history with environmental history. The availability of resources depends not only on the right to cross a border but also on the ecological effects of development and the governmental institutions responsible for resource management.

Economic integration does not necessarily weaken Indigenous citizenship or sovereignty. It may provide resources for community institutions and make transboundary relationships easier to maintain. Nevertheless, dependency on externally controlled markets, unequal access to resources and restrictions on movement may constrain the practical exercise of governmental authority. Students should distinguish the continuing political relationship between a person and an Indigenous nation from the economic capacity of a government or community. A community may maintain strong political identity despite severe economic constraints, while a successful enterprise does not automatically establish expanded territorial jurisdiction. This distinction is a central component of the chapter's analytical framework.

The costs imposed by border administration may also be cumulative. A household making occasional journeys faces a different economic problem from an enterprise dependent on regular deliveries. A cultural institution may have to arrange the movement of artists, teaching materials and community members across a border, while a commercial enterprise may face regulatory requirements concerning goods and transactions. In each case, the economic significance of the boundary depends on the frequency and purpose of movement. A historical account should consider how changes in administrative systems affect these different forms of economic organization over time.

Economic History Study — Barrier and connection

Border regulation changes the costs and possibilities of exchange, but cross-border employment and trade can also support Indigenous households and institutions. The Diabo case connects wage labor with admission law. The Kickapoo Act recognizes a different community-specific legal history. Economic participation is neither proof of assimilation nor a guarantee of institutional autonomy. [33][39]

  1. Explain how the regulation of goods can affect a business without preventing the owner from crossing.
  2. Identify a mechanism by which enterprise revenue might support community institutions.
  3. Distinguish economic integration from the authority to govern.
Section 142.16

International Borders, Natural Resources and Shared Ecosystems

Environmental systems routinely extend beyond international boundaries. The political jurisdiction responsible for a particular stretch of a river may differ from the jurisdiction governing the river's headwaters or the waters into which it flows. Fish and other migratory species may move through several governmental territories during their lifecycles. Pollution generated in one jurisdiction may affect communities in another. These conditions are particularly important for Indigenous peoples whose historical relationships with resources developed before the present international boundary and whose treaty or Aboriginal rights may be connected to specific harvesting areas.

The Columbia River Basin illustrates the scale of the problem. The river originates in Canada and flows into the United States, connecting an extensive system of tributaries and ecosystems. The Columbia River Treaty, signed in 1961 and brought into force in 1964, established a bilateral framework centered on flood control and hydroelectric power. Large dams and reservoirs profoundly transformed the river system, including fish habitats and Indigenous resource relationships. The original interstate arrangements did not give Indigenous governments an equivalent role as treaty parties. Indigenous peoples on both sides continued to pursue the protection and restoration of fisheries and cultural relationships with the basin. Chapter 120 examines the wider historical context of Indigenous water rights.

The Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission represents the four Columbia River treaty fishing tribes: the Yakama, Umatilla, Warm Springs and Nez Perce tribal governments. Their cooperative work concerns fisheries and the ecological conditions necessary to sustain them. In Canada, the Ktunaxa, Secwépemc and Syilx Okanagan Nations have participated as partners in the process of modernizing the Columbia River Treaty. The governments of Canada and the United States announced an agreement in principle in 2024 that proposed greater attention to ecosystem health and Indigenous cultural values, among other subjects. An agreement in principle must be distinguished from a completed treaty amendment and its implementation. The historical significance is the increasing prominence of Indigenous resource relationships in a bilateral framework initially focused on other objectives. [41][42]

The Sinixt case illustrates another dimension of resource access. In R. v. Desautel, 2021 SCC 17, Canada's Supreme Court considered the claim of a United States resident and citizen who was a member of the Lakes Tribe of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation and who hunted in the traditional territory of the Sinixt in British Columbia. The Court held that contemporary successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied what is now Canada before European contact can fall within the constitutional category of Aboriginal peoples of Canada even if they reside outside Canada. It upheld the recognition of the specific Aboriginal hunting right at issue. The decision did not establish a general immigration entitlement or unrestricted right to cross the border. It demonstrates how an Indigenous historical relationship can remain legally significant despite the modern international line. [43][44]

Other regional examples include the shared Great Lakes and St. Lawrence system, the Salish Sea, the Colorado River and the Arctic marine environment. Each poses different questions of authority. In the Colorado River basin, upstream diversions and water allocation affect the ecology of the delta, a continuing homeland of Cucapá communities. In the Salish Sea, salmon, shellfish and pollution cross state and provincial jurisdictions. In the Arctic, the changing conditions of sea ice affect movement and harvesting, while regulation of marine resources may involve multiple countries and Indigenous institutions. The issue is not simply a lack of environmental regulation but the need to coordinate regulation across a landscape whose ecological relationships do not match national boundaries.

Indigenous ecological knowledge and governmental participation can change the priorities of transboundary management. Resource restoration may be understood not only as the recovery of a commercially valuable species but also as the restoration of cultural and political relationships. The Buffalo Treaty provides an example of Indigenous governments organizing around a shared ecological responsibility. The Pikialasorsuaq initiatives similarly connect Inuit mobility with environmental stewardship. These cases show that international borders can create obstacles to shared-resource governance but can also become the subject of new institutional arrangements. The effectiveness of those arrangements depends on authority, funding, participation and the actual condition of the resources concerned.

The Desautel decision is also significant for comparison with Mitchell. Both involved Indigenous relationships crossing the United States–Canada boundary, and both were examined within Canada's constitutional framework for Aboriginal rights. But one concerned the particular assertion of duty-free importation for trade, while the other concerned a harvesting right in a traditional territory. The different outcomes cannot be explained by classifying one community as more legitimate than another. They reflect the different rights claimed, historical evidence and legal questions before the Court. A legal history that treats these cases as interchangeable would miss the central institutional distinction.

Environmental History Study — Shared ecosystems under divided authority

The Columbia River Basin crosses Canada and the United States; the original interstate treaty emphasized flood control and electricity. Indigenous fisheries and cultural values create additional governance objectives. The 2024 agreement in principle is a proposed modernization framework, not evidence that all changes have entered force. [41][42]

  2. Why might upstream decisions affect harvesting downstream?
  3. Compare a treaty fishing right, a cooperative restoration program and state resource jurisdiction.
Primary Source Window — R. v. Desautel (2021)

Context and source type: Canadian Supreme Court judgment involving a U.S.-resident member of the Lakes Tribe of the Colville Reservation and an asserted Sinixt hunting right.

Documentary paraphrase: The Court held that contemporary successor communities living outside Canada can fall within the constitutional category of Aboriginal peoples of Canada, and upheld the particular hunting right.

Analysis: The case demonstrates the continuing significance of historical territorial relationships despite present residence outside Canada.

Perspective and limitations: The decision does not resolve a general right of entry into Canada. The Court’s summary and the Sinixt community account have different purposes.

Division V

Indigenous Cooperation, Territorial Continuity and Sovereignty

Section 142.17

Indigenous Resistance and the Defense of Border-Crossing Rights

Indigenous peoples have challenged the administrative consequences of international boundaries through a variety of political strategies. Some claims invoke historical treaties, while others emphasize inherent rights grounded in Indigenous nationhood and territorial relationships. Governments and community organizations have pursued negotiations, public advocacy, litigation and arrangements for practical cooperation. These strategies have developed in response to different historical circumstances, and their outcomes should not be treated as interchangeable. A court judgment, a legislative amendment, a negotiated administrative practice and a political declaration may all be significant while carrying very different kinds of authority.

The northeastern borderlands illustrate the importance of treaty-based claims. Mohawk individuals and institutions have invoked the Jay Treaty and the history of movement across the international line. The litigation involving Paul Diabo in the 1920s was an important part of the history of United States recognition of Canadian-born Indigenous mobility. Later claims concerning the importation of goods, including Mitchell v. M.N.R., reveal how the movement of people and the movement of property became separate legal issues. The different outcomes demonstrate that Indigenous claims cannot be evaluated by referring to a single historical treaty without examining the legal framework in which the particular dispute arises. [33][40]

The northern Plains provide another context for political advocacy. The Blackfoot Confederacy encompasses nations operating under two national legal systems. Cooperation among its constituent nations can provide a way of articulating shared concerns without assuming that each has identical rights or governmental powers. The Buffalo Treaty is an example of an Indigenous initiative directed toward shared ecological, cultural and economic relationships. Other efforts may focus on the movement of community members, ceremonial obligations or the recognition of documents. The historical significance of these initiatives lies in the ability of Indigenous institutions to formulate political objectives that do not correspond neatly to the territorial categories of external governments. [20][21]

In the southern borderlands, the Tohono O'odham Nation has publicly opposed wall construction that it considers harmful to its territory while continuing to assert its responsibilities concerning public safety and cooperation with governmental authorities. This position illustrates the complexity of Indigenous resistance. A community may support particular forms of governmental cooperation and oppose other measures that constrain its authority or relationships. Treating resistance as an unconditional rejection of every state institution would obscure the specific political decisions being made. [25]

The Jay Treaty Border Alliance, formed in 2017 by tribal governments and First Nations, provides a more recent example of coordinated advocacy along the northern boundary. The Alliance describes its purpose in terms of the protection and advancement of Indigenous mobility rights and grounds that purpose in an interpretation of the Jay Treaty as recognition of an inherent right. Canadian government discussions through the Alliance's collaborative initiative have addressed practical and legislative issues. The existence of these discussions should not be mistaken for completed legislative reform. Rather, they illustrate how Indigenous political organizations can pursue changes to state institutions while maintaining their own understanding of the origin and nature of the rights at stake. [45][46][48][51]

For students, an important distinction is between historical recognition and legal creation. If an Indigenous nation maintains that a right preceded the state, a treaty may be understood as evidence that outsiders acknowledged the right. A domestic court or legislature may instead focus on the legal source through which the right is enforceable. These questions are not identical, and the historical analysis should not force Indigenous political claims into the categories of ordinary immigration law alone. Nor should it describe an asserted right as automatically enforceable without examining the applicable legal framework. The history of resistance is a history of communities negotiating both the practical circumstances of mobility and the political meaning of the boundary itself.

A political claim may remain important even before it results in a judicial decision or legislative amendment. Organizations can create a record of community concerns, articulate proposed reforms, develop shared positions and negotiate with administrative agencies. Such activity changes the political setting in which later legal decisions may be made. Historians should study the sequence from the formulation of a claim through coalition-building and institutional response, rather than treating a final statute or judgment as the only meaningful event. This approach also gives appropriate attention to Indigenous agency when the outcome of advocacy remains unresolved.

Historical Debate — Are mobility rights derived from states or inherent?

One approach examines Indigenous political authority and territorial relationships that existed before states. Another examines the legal sources through which domestic courts and agencies recognize and enforce particular rights. These are not simply mutually exclusive historical interpretations: a right may be understood as inherent by its holders and given a particular form of enforceability under state law. The disagreement concerns the relationship between political origin, legal recognition and practical implementation.

  1. What is the difference between the origin of a claimed right and its domestic enforceability?
  2. Compare a political declaration, a court decision and a statute as evidence.
  3. How does the Jay Treaty Border Alliance describe its objectives?
Section 142.18

Transboundary Indigenous Governance and Institutional Cooperation

Transboundary governance refers to the coordination of institutions across a boundary. It does not necessarily create a single government or a unified legal jurisdiction. Indigenous peoples have developed such arrangements to address problems that cannot be resolved adequately within one national administrative system. These problems may concern shared resources, family relationships, cultural education, economic development, public services and the assertion of political rights. The form of cooperation depends on the history and objectives of the participating communities and on the legal environment in which each institution operates.

At Akwesasne, different Indigenous governmental institutions operate in the northern and southern portions of the community, while traditional political structures also remain significant. The Mohawk Council of Akwesasne and the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe each have responsibilities within their respective governmental frameworks. Cooperation can concern issues affecting the wider community, even when the authority of each institution differs. The presence of several governmental structures does not imply that Akwesasne lacks political continuity. Instead, it demonstrates the institutional complexity produced by an international boundary superimposed on an Indigenous community. Akwesasne's court and police institutions also illustrate the need to understand the relationship between Indigenous law and the surrounding legal systems. [16][17][18][19]

The Buffalo Treaty, first signed in 2014, represents a different form of cooperation. Indigenous nations articulated shared responsibilities concerning the restoration of buffalo and the cultural, ecological, educational and economic relationships associated with them. Its articles establish objectives for cooperation and knowledge-sharing under the authority and ethical standards of the participating nations. This is an Indigenous treaty, rather than an interstate agreement that transfers territorial sovereignty between Canada and the United States. It illustrates the capacity of Indigenous governments to develop political relationships across the international boundary on the basis of their own priorities. Implementing buffalo restoration can also require coordination with landowners and governmental agencies responsible for particular areas. [21][22]

In the Pacific Northwest, the Coast Salish Gathering provides a forum for cooperation on environmental priorities in the Salish Sea region. Its work reflects the relationships of Coast Salish peoples with interconnected marine and watershed systems. The Gathering's institutional form differs from an agreement establishing a single governmental jurisdiction. Its significance lies in the ability of Indigenous leaders to identify common concerns and engage other governmental actors within a regional framework that reflects Indigenous geography. A cooperative forum can influence policy without replacing the existing authority of each participating nation or government. [23][24]

In the Arctic, the Pikialasorsuaq Commission and related initiatives illustrate the interaction of community consultation, environmental protection and Indigenous mobility. Inuit organizations have advocated for a regional management approach that reflects the shared importance of the polynya to communities in Canada and Greenland. The participation of the governments of Canada, Greenland and Denmark in subsequent discussions demonstrates the importance of cooperation across different constitutional and territorial arrangements. Such initiatives should be evaluated through their actual institutional powers, proposed objectives and implementation rather than assuming that every declaration immediately changes domestic law. [30][31]

The Jay Treaty Border Alliance offers an additional model: a coalition focused on shared mobility concerns rather than the management of one ecosystem or the governance of a single divided community. Its stated governance includes representation from Indigenous governments on both sides of the United States–Canada border. Through a collaborative initiative with Canadian governmental institutions, it has participated in policy discussions concerning mobility and the movement of goods. These efforts represent the development of an institutional capacity to engage with national administrations. They also show why Indigenous cross-border cooperation is not merely a consequence of state policy; it is an active political strategy pursued by Indigenous governments. [45][46][48][51]

Institutional cooperation involves decisions about representation. A joint body must determine which communities participate, what responsibilities it accepts, how decisions are made and how its work relates to the authority of participating governments. The Jay Treaty Border Alliance's governance arrangements, which include co-chairs representing First Nations and tribal governments on opposite sides of the boundary, illustrate one response to this problem. Such organizational design matters because a cooperative institution cannot automatically speak for every Indigenous people affected by an international boundary. Its authority and significance should be understood through the participation and objectives of its members. [48]

Institutional Study — Cooperation across multiple jurisdictions

Compare Akwesasne’s local institutions, the Buffalo Treaty, Coast Salish Gathering and the Jay Treaty Border Alliance. Each addresses a different type of shared problem. Cooperative bodies vary in their membership, decision-making authority, objectives and relationship to states. Their existence does not imply a unified jurisdiction. [16][21][23][45]

  1. Classify each example as a local governmental arrangement, Indigenous treaty, forum or advocacy coalition.
  2. Explain what evidence would establish the actual authority of each body.
  3. Why might an environmental cooperation initiative need different participants from a mobility advocacy coalition?
Historical Vocabulary — Transboundary governance

Definition: Institutional coordination among governments or communities across a boundary.

Historical context: The Buffalo Treaty and Jay Treaty Border Alliance illustrate different objectives.

Significance and potential misunderstanding: A joint institution need not exercise a single unified jurisdiction or represent every Indigenous nation.

Primary Source Window — The Buffalo Treaty (2014)

Context and source type: Treaty developed by Indigenous nations, first signed in Montana in 2014, concerning restoration of relationships with buffalo.

Documentary paraphrase: Its articles address cooperation in conservation, culture, economics, health, education and research, with knowledge-sharing subject to the participating nations’ own standards.

Analysis: The treaty expresses Indigenous governmental agency across an international boundary and links ecological restoration to social and cultural relationships.

Perspective and limitations: It establishes commitments among participants, not a state-to-state territorial transfer. Implementation depends on further decisions, resources and legal arrangements.

Section 142.19

Comparative Models of Indigenous Transboundary Continuity

The historical cases developed in this chapter can be compared through the Six-Dimension Indigenous Borderlands Governance Framework. The first dimension, territorial fragmentation, asks whether an international line divided an established homeland, intersected a regional network, or later affected a community formed through migration. The Tohono O'odham and Kumeyaay histories illustrate the division of established territories. Kickapoo history illustrates a transnational community whose present geography reflects migration and reconstruction. Akwesasne shows how international and subnational lines can intersect the territory of a single community. These different histories caution against treating all transboundary peoples as examples of an identical process.

The second dimension concerns legal and political jurisdiction. Akwesasne offers a particularly complex example because Indigenous governmental structures operate alongside the jurisdictions of Canada, the United States, Ontario, Quebec and New York. The Blackfoot Confederacy encompasses four nations with governmental relationships to different states. Inuit communities in Alaska, Canada and Greenland operate under different constitutional arrangements. In each case, political and cultural relationships extend beyond the jurisdiction of a particular government. Comparative analysis must therefore distinguish the authority of individual institutions from the broader identity and history of the peoples concerned.

Mobility and administration form the third dimension. The Jay Treaty and later United States legislation provide one historical and statutory framework affecting qualifying Canadian-born Indigenous people. Canada's entry law differs. The Texas Band of Kickapoo Act provides a particular southern borderlands arrangement. Bering Strait history demonstrates how geopolitical restrictions can disrupt family relationships even without a terrestrial barrier. The difference among these cases is not a difference in the inherent worth of the communities concerned. It concerns the historical development of state institutions and the forms of political response available to Indigenous peoples.

Economic and resource access, the fourth dimension, reveals the ways in which political geography intersects with material conditions. The Columbia River, the Salish Sea and Pikialasorsuaq are ecological systems extending across jurisdictions. Indigenous harvesting rights and environmental responsibilities may depend on particular legal arrangements as well as on the condition of the ecosystem itself. The Buffalo Treaty demonstrates another approach to the restoration of a shared ecological relationship. A comparison of economic and resource access should ask what resources are involved, which institutions exercise authority, and how Indigenous governments seek to sustain those relationships.

Family and cultural continuity and transboundary institutional cooperation constitute the final two dimensions. They are closely connected but not identical. Kinship relationships can persist without a formal intergovernmental agreement. A language program or community organization may maintain ties across a border even when its members operate under separate legal systems. Formal cooperation can provide resources and institutional support for those relationships. The Jay Treaty Border Alliance, Coast Salish Gathering and Buffalo Treaty illustrate distinct forms of organized cooperation, while the Bering Strait reconnection demonstrates how personal and family relationships can give broader political and cultural significance to international contact.

The purpose of the framework is comparative historical reasoning. It does not define Indigenous sovereignty, determine political legitimacy or assign a score to a people. Students should use it to identify what differs among historical circumstances and what forms of continuity remain possible. The same community may exhibit several models at once: a divided homeland may also experience migration, maintain maritime relationships and develop cooperative institutions. No single legal classification or political arrangement can encompass all of these processes. The comparative matrix is a starting point for examining relationships, not a substitute for the distinct history of each community.

The comparison can be extended to the types of historical evidence needed for each dimension. Treaty texts and maps may illuminate territorial changes, but they do not by themselves explain family continuity. Governmental constitutions and court judgments reveal aspects of jurisdiction, but they may not capture how community institutions actually operate. Oral histories and public community records may illuminate cultural relationships, while ecological evidence can help explain changes in resource access. The framework therefore encourages students to combine evidence rather than use a single category of source to answer every question.

Comparative Historical Study — Models of transboundary continuity

Apply all six dimensions of the framework to at least two case studies. The comparative matrix distinguishes the histories of divided homelands, migration, maritime relationships and cooperation. A community can exhibit multiple patterns simultaneously. Differences in governmental powers or legal recognition are not rankings of Indigenous legitimacy.
