Section 142.20

International Borders and the Future of Indigenous Sovereignty

International boundaries have become central institutions of modern North American political geography. They establish the territorial frameworks within which state governments exercise authority, regulate entry and commerce, and administer resources and public services. Their historical development, however, must be understood in relation to the Indigenous societies whose territories and relationships they intersect. Agreements among states did not necessarily reflect the consent of Indigenous peoples, and subsequent processes of surveying, settlement and administration accumulated their effects over time. The boundary was a historical transformation rather than an inevitable feature of the landscape.

The experience of divided homelands reveals the importance of distinguishing political geography from political membership. Indigenous citizenship may extend beyond the territory over which a government exercises recognized jurisdiction. A community may maintain ceremonial, familial and economic relationships with places that lie in another state. Migration can create new centers of Indigenous life without terminating earlier relationships. These realities do not mean that state jurisdiction lacks practical force. They show that the historical and political geography of Indigenous nationhood cannot be represented solely by the international map of modern states.

The legal history examined in this chapter demonstrates how states have responded to Indigenous mobility in different ways. The Jay Treaty, Section 289 of the United States Immigration and Nationality Act, Canadian entry law and the Texas Band of Kickapoo Act represent different institutional arrangements. Litigation over customs and harvesting rights further illustrates the importance of the precise issue and legal framework involved. Recognition of a particular right does not resolve every question of Indigenous mobility, and rejection of a particular claim does not determine the legitimacy of all Indigenous territorial relationships. Historical analysis must maintain the distinction between Indigenous political claims and the domestic legal mechanisms through which some of those claims are recognized.

The experience of resource governance further reveals that the operation of international boundaries affects more than the relationship between an individual traveler and an immigration officer. Communities depend on ecosystems, economic relationships and institutions that may extend across national territories. The capacity to restore resources, provide services and maintain cultural institutions can depend on cooperation with neighboring communities and governments. Indigenous political agency is visible in the development of institutions such as the Buffalo Treaty, the Coast Salish Gathering and the Jay Treaty Border Alliance. These arrangements do not all have the same legal character, but each illustrates a form of political initiative directed toward relationships that exceed the international boundary.

The future of Indigenous sovereignty cannot be predicted from the history of boundaries alone. States continue to exercise territorial and administrative authority, while Indigenous peoples continue to articulate their rights, responsibilities and political relationships. Future arrangements will depend on historical circumstances, political decisions, legal developments and the institutional capacities of the peoples and governments involved. A historical account should explain these possibilities without treating the disappearance of borders, complete assimilation or any other outcome as inevitable. The central conclusion is that Indigenous nationhood remains a continuing political and historical reality within a continent organized by states whose boundaries were established much later.

Chapter 143 broadens the scale of inquiry. Whereas this chapter has concentrated on relationships across particular international boundaries, the next examines international Indigenous diplomacy, organizations and movements. Those institutions bring together peoples whose territories may be geographically distant but whose political concerns intersect. The transition from borderlands cooperation to Indigenous internationalism is therefore a transition in scale and institutional form, not a departure from the central historical question of how Indigenous nations act within and beyond the political frameworks imposed upon them.

A final distinction is between sovereignty as a political principle and capacity as the practical means of exercising authority. Indigenous governments may retain political relationships and claims despite limited resources or restrictions imposed by other governments. Institutional cooperation can increase the capacity to address particular problems without resolving every territorial or legal dispute. Recognizing this distinction enables historians to describe the persistence of Indigenous nationhood without minimizing the consequences of dispossession or administrative constraint. It also avoids the assumption that only a political community with an internationally recognized state can exercise meaningful governmental authority.

Continuity and Change Over Time — From imposed boundaries to cooperation

International treaties, surveys and administrative systems transformed the territorial and legal circumstances of Indigenous peoples. Family, cultural and political relationships persisted or were reconstructed in different ways. Cooperative institutions emerged in response to particular historical problems. Neither the persistence of a relationship nor the creation of a new institution proves that all constraints have disappeared.

  1. Identify one continuity and one transformation in each of two case studies.
  2. Explain how institutional cooperation can strengthen capacity without unifying jurisdiction.
  3. How does the chapter prepare for the study of Indigenous internationalism in Chapter 143?

Chapter Summary

International borders in North America emerged through diplomatic settlements among colonial powers and successor states. They did not originate as agreements among all the Indigenous peoples whose territories they affected. The practical authority of these borders developed through surveys, settlement, land policy, legislation and administrative institutions. A distinction between international territorial claims and Indigenous territorial relationships is therefore necessary to understand the historical consequences of state formation.

Indigenous territorial systems existed long before modern states. They involved political authority, resource access, negotiated relationships, settlement and mobility. Such arrangements differed among communities and changed over time. International borders intersected these older relationships, sometimes dividing established homelands and sometimes affecting networks created through displacement and migration. A map of contemporary state or Indigenous administrative boundaries cannot fully represent these histories.

The United States–Canada boundary developed through several diplomatic settlements. Communities along the Great Lakes, northern Plains and Pacific Northwest experienced its consequences in different ways. Akwesasne illustrates the complex interaction of Indigenous, national and subnational jurisdictions. The Blackfoot Confederacy demonstrates how related nations can maintain political cooperation while operating under different legal systems. Coast Salish communities maintain relationships in an interconnected marine environment divided by national boundaries.

The southern and Arctic borderlands provide important comparisons. O'odham and Kumeyaay homelands were divided by the United States–Mexico boundary, whereas the present transnational Kickapoo community reflects historical migration and reconstruction. The Bering Strait and Aleutian region demonstrate how international boundaries can interrupt maritime relationships, including those created or transformed through colonial relocation. The 1988 Friendship Flight illustrates a major moment of renewed contact after Cold War separation.

The legal history of the Jay Treaty demonstrates the need to distinguish treaty provisions from modern domestic legislation and judicial interpretation. The United States protects passage for a particular statutory class of Canadian-born Indigenous persons under Section 289 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Canada's entry framework differs. The Texas Band of Kickapoo Act provides a specific arrangement for a particular community. No one of these legal instruments establishes identical rights for every Indigenous person across all borders.

Indigenous citizenship and state citizenship are distinct political and legal relationships. Registration under Canadian federal law and ancestry-based eligibility under United States immigration law cannot be treated as interchangeable with membership determined by Indigenous governments. Documentary requirements make these distinctions consequential in daily life. The relationship among identity, political membership and legal status must be examined without adopting external administrative categories as the measure of Indigenous nationhood.

Customs and immigration systems regulate different subjects. The ability of an individual to enter a country does not automatically establish an entitlement to import goods free of duties or other restrictions. Canadian litigation in Francis and Mitchell illustrates the importance of distinguishing treaty-based and constitutionally grounded claims. These judgments must be interpreted according to the particular legal issues and evidence before the courts, rather than generalized into conclusions about every Indigenous mobility or commercial right.

International boundaries affect family relationships, employment, economic capacity and environmental stewardship. Repeated journeys may be necessary for responsibilities that do not fit conventional definitions of immigration or tourism. Economic integration can strengthen institutions but can also expose communities to dependency and regulatory constraints. Shared ecosystems such as the Columbia River Basin demonstrate the mismatch between political jurisdictions and ecological relationships, while the Desautel case shows the continuing legal significance of historical territorial relationships across a border.

Indigenous nations have responded to these circumstances through advocacy, legal claims, negotiation and institutional cooperation. The Buffalo Treaty, the Coast Salish Gathering, the Jay Treaty Border Alliance and Inuit initiatives concerning Pikialasorsuaq illustrate different forms of organized political action. They do not establish one uniform model of governance. Their significance lies in the capacity of communities to formulate collective objectives that exceed the territorial categories of modern states.

The history of international borders therefore reveals a continuing interaction between state jurisdiction and Indigenous nationhood. Political membership, territorial authority, institutional capacity and cultural continuity are related but distinct. The Six-Dimension Framework provides a method for comparing these relationships without ranking Indigenous peoples. Chapter 143 will examine how Indigenous political cooperation extends beyond the immediate geography of divided homelands into wider international institutions and movements.

Key Terms

International boundary
A line or zone separating state jurisdictions, established by agreement or practice. A line in a treaty acquires practical force through surveying, administration and enforcement.
Indigenous homeland
Territory with which an Indigenous people maintains historical, political, cultural or economic relationships, even if occupation or recognized control has been disrupted.
Territorial fragmentation
Reorganization or division of a homeland, including by international boundaries or colonial land policies.
Jurisdiction
Authority to make and enforce law. It may be limited by territory, subject matter or the legal status of persons.
Sovereignty
Political authority of a people or government; Indigenous sovereignty need not imply independent statehood.
Territorial authority
Control exercised over a defined space.
Borderlands
Regions shaped by proximity to a boundary.
Transboundary community
A community with ties across a boundary.
Indigenous citizenship
Membership in an Indigenous nation under its own law. It can extend to members living beyond a government’s recognized territory.
State citizenship
Legal membership in a modern state. It is administered under national law and is not a substitute for Indigenous membership.
Nationality
Legal membership or national affiliation in international law; distinguish from Indigenous citizenship.
Residency
Actual residence in a place, or, in immigration law, a legally defined status permitting residence; context determines the meaning.
Immigration
Movement into another country for residence; immigration law regulates admission, residence and related status.
Customs
State regulation and taxation of goods crossing a boundary. Customs rules concern goods, duties and import restrictions, distinct from personal admission.
Border-crossing rights
Legal entitlements to cross under particular instruments, distinct from discretionary permissions and Indigenous claims of inherent mobility.
Treaty rights
Rights secured or recognized in a treaty; their domestic enforceability depends on the applicable legal framework.
Inherent rights
Rights understood as originating in Indigenous peoples’ own political existence and relationships rather than as gifts from states; domestic recognition varies.
Federal recognition
Formal U.S. acknowledgment of a tribal political relationship, not the origin of Indigenous nationhood. The U.S. classification differs from Mexican constitutional recognition and Canadian Indian Act registration.
Identification documents
Credentials issued by states or Indigenous governments.
Administrative discretion
Official latitude in applying rules.
Seasonal mobility
Recurrent movement tied to resources or work.
Maritime boundary
A line dividing sea jurisdictions. It can concern different forms of authority over waters or seabed, not necessarily all aspects of mobility.
Shared watershed
A drainage area crossing a boundary.
Transboundary governance
Coordination across jurisdictions. Examples include joint stewardship bodies and Indigenous political alliances; coordination does not necessarily unify jurisdiction.
Political continuity
Persistence or reconstruction of political relationships, institutions and community membership over time.
Reserve / reservation
Territories set aside or recognized under Canadian or United States law; their extent and jurisdiction need not correspond to historical homelands.
Jay Treaty
1794 Anglo-American treaty relevant to Indigenous mobility.
Canadian Indian status
Legal status under Canada's Indian Act.
Tribal enrollment
Membership under a tribal nation's criteria.
Cultural property
Objects or materials significant to a community’s cultural heritage; applicable legal protections and restrictions vary.
Multilocal residence
Actually living in more than one location over a period, distinct from maintaining ties to other places.
Cold War Arctic restrictions
Limits on Bering Strait movement.
Intergovernmental agreement
Formal arrangement between governments.
Territorial transfer
State-to-state cession not implying Indigenous consent.
Ecological knowledge
Place-based environmental understanding.

Review Materials

Major People, Communities, Institutions and Places

Akwesasne
Mohawk community spanning New York, Ontario and Quebec; illustrates a divided homeland and multiple jurisdictions.
Mohawk Council of Akwesasne
Elected governmental institution for the northern portion of Akwesasne; develops community law and services.
Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe
Federally recognized tribal government serving the southern portion of Akwesasne in New York.
Mohawk Nation Council of Chiefs
Traditional Mohawk political institution; distinguishes Haudenosaunee governance from contemporary state-recognized administrative bodies.
Haudenosaunee Confederacy
Confederated political tradition of six nations whose relationships extend across the northern boundary.
Anishinaabe peoples
Related but politically diverse peoples including Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi, with histories across the Great Lakes.
Blackfoot Confederacy
Four nations: Siksika, Kainai, Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni (Blackfeet); political relationships across Alberta and Montana.
Métis
Distinct Indigenous people with historical communities and political networks linked to the fur trade and Plains; not a synonym for mixed ancestry.
Cree, Assiniboine and Dakota/Lakota communities
Distinct peoples with histories of mobility, diplomacy and displacement across the northern Plains; not one political unit.
Coast Salish peoples
Diverse Indigenous peoples of the Salish Sea region, whose marine, family and political networks cross the northern boundary.
Tohono O’odham
Sonoran Desert people whose homeland intersects the U.S.–Mexico border; the Nation in Arizona is a distinct governmental institution.
Kumeyaay / Kumiai
Related communities of southern California and northern Baja California with divided homeland relationships.
Kickapoo
Algonquian-speaking people whose migration produced a transnational community with important connections between Texas and Coahuila.
Yaqui / Yoeme
People of Sonora with communities in Arizona, whose cross-border relations reflect territorial attachment, displacement and migration.
Inuit
Peoples across Alaska, Canada and Greenland with related but distinct regional institutions and languages; broader political usages vary.
Yupik and Iñupiat
Distinct Arctic peoples; Siberian Yupik networks across the Bering Strait are central to the history of Cold War separation.
Unangan / Unangax̂
Indigenous maritime people of the Aleutian region, with historical connections to the Pribilof and Commander islands.
Tartupaluk (Hans Island)
Island in Nares Strait addressed by the 2022 Canada–Denmark–Greenland boundary agreement, with provisions for Inuit access.
Pikialasorsuaq
North Water polynya between northern Canadian and Greenlandic Inuit communities; focus of Inuit-led stewardship and mobility initiatives.
Bering Strait
Maritime passage separating Alaska and the Russian Far East; historically connected neighboring Indigenous communities.
Jay Treaty (1794)
Anglo-American agreement whose Article III addressed passage and trade; central to subsequent Indigenous mobility claims.
Jay Treaty Border Alliance
Coalition formed in 2017 to advocate for Indigenous mobility rights along the United States–Canada boundary.
Buffalo Treaty
Indigenous treaty first signed in 2014; cooperative commitments to restoring relationships with buffalo.
Columbia River Basin
Shared river system with major Indigenous fisheries and cultural relationships affected by bilateral resource management.
Sinixt
People of the Columbia region; the Desautel judgment recognized the specific Aboriginal hunting right at issue despite the claimant’s U.S. residence.

Extended Writing Prompts

  1. Historical causation: Explain how diplomacy, surveying, settlement and administrative institutions transformed Indigenous territorial geography. Use at least two regions and distinguish territorial claims from Indigenous consent.
  2. Comparative history: Compare Akwesasne and Tohono O’odham communities as examples of divided homelands. Consider jurisdiction, mobility and practical effects of the line.
  3. Legal and institutional history: Compare the Jay Treaty, Section 289, Canada’s entry law and the Kickapoo statute. Explain the difference between treaty claims, statutory eligibility, Indigenous citizenship and admission.
  4. Economic and environmental history: Explain how international boundaries affect Indigenous commerce and shared resources, using the Columbia River or Salish Sea and at least one example of Indigenous institutional cooperation.
  5. Historical argument: Assess the limitations of explaining Indigenous nationhood solely through the territorial framework of modern states. Use specific evidence and acknowledge the continuing practical authority of state institutions.

Comparative Historical Exercises

  1. Northern and southern boundaries: select Akwesasne and Tohono O’odham. Construct a two-column timeline and compare the legal history, geography, administrative restrictions, and institutional responses; distinguish observed facts from interpretation.
  2. Divided homelands and migrant communities: compare a Haudenosaunee or O’odham example with the Kickapoo. Explain the different historical routes to transnational community, and compare the scope of the relevant legal arrangements without ranking legitimacy.
  3. Land and maritime boundaries: compare one northern or southern land-border case with the Bering Strait or Canada–Greenland region. Use the maps, treaty records and community accounts to examine mobility, resource access, and institutional responses.

Research or Library Extension

Research or Library Extension

One Homeland, Multiple Jurisdictions — An Indigenous International Boundary Study

Select one community studied in this chapter. Construct an evidence-based dossier explaining how international boundary formation changed its political and social geography. Use public sources, including the community’s own publications where available. Distinguish contemporary territorial jurisdiction, historical relationships, and legal claims.

  1. Prepare an annotated geographic reference map. Identify modern political boundaries, selected places and the limits of the historical evidence; avoid asserting exclusive territorial boundaries without support.
  2. Build a timeline of boundary agreements, later administrative changes and community responses. Distinguish dates of agreement from implementation.
  3. Identify Indigenous governmental and community institutions. Describe their authority and the sources that establish it.
  4. Compare the relevant national legal frameworks, separating treaty, statute, court decision and administrative practice. Do not give personal travel or legal advice.
  5. Analyze kinship, mobility, economic relationships and resource access using the six dimensions of the chapter framework.
  6. Identify a concrete example of Indigenous advocacy or institutional cooperation. Distinguish an announced objective from a completed legal or institutional change.
  7. Conclude with a supported historical argument. Include a bibliography with title, author or institution, date if available, and source location.

Assessment: geographic accuracy, historical chronology, appropriate distinctions among legal instruments, source criticism, Indigenous historical agency and the quality of comparative analysis. Do not seek restricted ceremonial knowledge or private crossing records.

Chapter Reflection

The international border often appears on maps as a permanent feature, but its historical significance lies in the processes through which it was created and administered. The diplomatic act of drawing a line, the survey of the landscape, the construction of state institutions and the regulation of movement represent different stages of a historical transformation. Studying them separately helps explain why an agreement concluded in the nineteenth century can acquire new consequences in the twentieth or twenty-first century.

Indigenous territorial relationships reveal the limitations of organizing history entirely around national states. A community's political geography may encompass places governed under several legal systems. Its members may maintain relationships across a border that appears to divide them into separate populations in national statistics. Such continuity does not erase the costs of dispossession, restrictions or unequal access to institutions. It demonstrates why historians must examine Indigenous political agency alongside the consequences of colonial and state expansion.

The legal cases in this chapter also illustrate the importance of historical evidence. Treaties, statutes and judgments establish particular claims and legal outcomes, but they do not provide a complete account of community experience. Indigenous governmental statements and community histories can illuminate the meaning of territorial relationships that state sources omit. A careful historian must understand the purpose and limitations of each source and recognize that political claims, legal recognition and historical interpretation are distinct questions.

The institutional examples offer a further lesson. Cooperation across a border does not necessarily require the abolition of that border or the creation of a single government. Indigenous nations have pursued shared ecological responsibilities, cultural programs and political advocacy through varied forms of organization. The effectiveness of these arrangements depends on their actual authority and resources, while their existence demonstrates the continuing capacity of Indigenous peoples to shape the institutions affecting their relationships.

Chapter 142 thus links the regional histories of divided and migrant communities with the broader history of Indigenous internationalism. Chapter 143 will examine the organizations and diplomatic movements through which Indigenous peoples participate in wider political relationships. The transition reinforces the central argument of the textbook: Indigenous nations are continuing historical and political communities whose institutions are indispensable to understanding North America, rather than remnants of a past superseded by modern states.

Sources and Further Reading

Historical legal provisions are discussed for educational purposes; the chapter is not legal or immigration advice. Modern arrangements are identified by the date of the cited record, and proposals are distinguished from completed implementation.
